title: Python Best Practices
description: PEP 8 style conventions, code organization, error handling, documentation, and habits that keep Python code maintainable.
objectives: Follow PEP 8 naming and style conventions
Organize code into reusable, well-scoped functions and modules
Apply sound error-handling and documentation habits

content.heading: Style, Naming, and Organization
content.body:
PEP 8 is Python's official style guide; following it (or an automated formatter that enforces it, like black) keeps code consistent and easier for others to read. Its core conventions: snake_case for variables and functions, PascalCase for classes, UPPER_SNAKE_CASE for constants, 4 spaces per indentation level (never tabs), and a soft line-length limit (traditionally 79 characters, though many teams now use 88-100). Meaningful names matter more than brevity — a variable named remaining_attempts is far clearer than n or x2.

Code organization means breaking a program into small, focused functions that each do one clear thing (making them easier to test and reuse), grouping related functions/classes into modules, and avoiding one giant script with everything at module/global scope.

content.heading: Error Handling, Documentation, and Avoiding Common Mistakes
content.body:
Prefer specific exception handling over bare except:, and validate inputs early with clear error messages rather than letting a cryptic exception surface deep inside unrelated code. Write docstrings for public functions, classes, and modules explaining what they do, their parameters, and their return value — this both documents the code and integrates with tools like help(). Avoid global mutable state where possible; passing data explicitly through function parameters and return values makes code easier to reason about and test than functions that silently read/modify shared globals.

Testing concepts matter even for small projects: writing simple test functions (with the standard library's unittest, or the popular third-party pytest) that check a function's behavior against known inputs/outputs catches regressions early and documents intended behavior. Common beginner mistakes worth actively avoiding: mutable default arguments (def f(items=[]):, which is shared across calls — use None and create the list inside the function instead), shadowing built-in names (list = [1,2,3] hides the built-in list type), and comparing to None with == instead of the idiomatic is None.

content.explanation: MAX_RETRIES follows the UPPER_SNAKE_CASE constant convention. fetch_user has a docstring explaining its contract. add_item avoids the classic mutable-default-argument pitfall by defaulting to None and creating a fresh list inside the function.

keyPoints: PEP 8 governs naming (snake_case/PascalCase/UPPER_SNAKE_CASE) and formatting conventions
Small, focused functions and well-organized modules are easier to test, reuse, and reason about
Prefer specific exception handling and clear docstrings over bare excepts and undocumented functions
Avoid mutable default arguments, shadowing built-in names, and unnecessary global mutable state
commonMistakes: Using a mutable object (list, dict) as a default argument value
Comparing to None with == instead of the idiomatic is None
Writing large, unfocused functions that do many unrelated things, making testing and reuse difficult
